notes.title: Operating Systems - Process Scheduling
notes.markdown:
# Operating Systems - Process Scheduling

## What the lecture covered

The scheduler decides which ready process gets the CPU next. Every policy is a trade-off between throughput, latency and fairness — there is no single best answer.

## Key algorithms

### First Come First Served (FCFS)

- Non-preemptive, runs processes in arrival order.
- Simple, but suffers from the **convoy effect**: one long job at the head of the queue stalls every short job behind it.

### Shortest Job First (SJF)

- Provably optimal for average waiting time.
- Impractical on its own — the scheduler cannot know burst times in advance, so real systems *estimate* them with an exponential average.

### Round Robin (RR)

- Preemptive FCFS with a time quantum `q`.
- Choosing `q` is the whole game:
  - `q` too large -> degenerates into FCFS
  - `q` too small -> context-switch overhead dominates
- Rule of thumb: 80% of CPU bursts should finish inside one quantum.

### Multilevel Feedback Queue

What Linux, Windows and macOS actually approximate. A process starts in a high-priority short-quantum queue and is demoted as it uses more CPU, so interactive work stays responsive while batch work still makes progress.

## Comparison

| Algorithm | Preemptive | Starvation risk | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| FCFS | No | Low | Batch systems |
| SJF | Optional | High | Known burst lengths |
| Round Robin | Yes | None | Time sharing |
| Priority | Optional | High (needs ageing) | Real-time-ish workloads |

## Worked example

Three processes arrive at t=0 with bursts 24, 3, 3 ms. Under FCFS the average waiting time is (0 + 24 + 27) / 3 = **17 ms**. Reorder them shortest-first and it drops to (0 + 3 + 6) / 3 = **3 ms** — same work, same CPU, five times better latency.

## Exam pointers

1. Be able to draw the Gantt chart before computing averages.
2. Waiting time = turnaround time - burst time.
3. Starvation is solved by **ageing**, not by raising the quantum.

notes.title: Data Structures - Balanced Trees
notes.markdown:
# Data Structures - Balanced Trees

## Why balance matters

A binary search tree gives `O(log n)` lookup only while it stays bushy. Insert already-sorted keys into a plain BST and it degenerates into a linked list — `O(n)` per operation. Balanced trees add a rebalancing rule so the height stays `O(log n)` no matter the insert order.

## AVL trees

- Invariant: for every node, `|height(left) - height(right)| <= 1`.
- Rebalanced with four rotation cases: LL, RR, LR, RL.
- Strictly balanced, so lookups are fast, but inserts/deletes rotate more often.

## Red-black trees

- Weaker invariant: no red node has a red child, and every root-to-leaf path has the same number of black nodes.
- Height is at most `2 * log2(n + 1)` — slightly taller than AVL, but far fewer rotations per write.
- This is why `std::map`, `TreeMap` and the Linux CFS scheduler all use red-black trees.

## Choosing between them

| | AVL | Red-black |
|---|---|---|
| Lookup | Faster | Slightly slower |
| Insert / delete | More rotations | Fewer rotations |
| Typical use | Read-heavy indexes | General purpose maps |

## B-trees, briefly

When the data lives on disk, the cost is dominated by block reads, not comparisons. A B-tree of order `m` stores up to `m-1` keys per node so one disk block answers many comparisons at once. That is the entire reason database indexes are B+ trees rather than red-black trees.

## Things worth memorising

1. A rotation is a **local** pointer rewrite — it never touches more than three nodes.
2. Rebalancing after an insert costs at most one rotation in a red-black tree.
3. Deletion is the hard case in every balanced tree; know at least one worked example.

notes.title: Microeconomics - Elasticity of Demand
notes.markdown:
# Microeconomics - Elasticity of Demand

## Definition

Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly quantity demanded reacts to a price change:

`Ed = (% change in quantity demanded) / (% change in price)`

Because the two move in opposite directions, `Ed` is negative — by convention we discuss its absolute value.

## Reading the number

| Value | Name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `|Ed| > 1` | Elastic | Buyers are price sensitive |
| `|Ed| = 1` | Unit elastic | Revenue unchanged by price moves |
| `|Ed| < 1` | Inelastic | Buyers keep buying anyway |

## What makes demand elastic

1. **Substitutes available** — the single biggest factor.
2. **Share of income** — a costlier item gets more scrutiny.
3. **Necessity vs luxury** — insulin is inelastic, cruises are not.
4. **Time horizon** — demand is almost always more elastic in the long run, because buyers can restructure their habits.

## Link to revenue

Total revenue = price x quantity. If demand is elastic, a price *cut* raises revenue; if inelastic, a price *rise* raises revenue. This single relationship explains most real pricing decisions.
